title: Lesson 10 · Building Sentences & the Interjection
blurb: Simple/compound/complex sentences, principal vs subordinate clauses, interjections, and the eight parts of speech.

items.prompt:
Is this sentence simple (one statement) or compound (two joined statements)?

“Birds sing.”
items.explain: One subject and one predicate — a simple sentence.

items.prompt:
Is this sentence simple (one statement) or compound (two joined statements)?

“Birds sing, and flowers bloom.”
items.explain: Two complete statements joined by “and” — a compound sentence.

items.prompt:
Is this sentence simple (one statement) or compound (two joined statements)?

“The dog barked loudly.”
items.explain: One statement — a simple sentence.

items.prompt:
Is this sentence simple (one statement) or compound (two joined statements)?

“Rain fell, but we stayed dry.”
items.explain: Two complete statements joined by “but” — a compound sentence.

items.prompt:
Is this sentence simple (one statement) or compound (two joined statements)?

“Snow is white.”
items.explain: One statement — a simple sentence.

items.prompt:
Is this sentence simple (one statement) or compound (two joined statements)?

“I came, and I saw.”
items.explain: Two complete statements joined by “and” — a compound sentence.

items.prompt:
Is this sentence simple (one statement) or compound (two joined statements)?

“Fish swim in the sea.”
items.explain: One statement — a simple sentence.

items.prompt:
Is this sentence simple (one statement) or compound (two joined statements)?

“He ran, so he won.”
items.explain: Two complete statements joined by “so” — a compound sentence.

items.prompt:
Is this clause principal (makes sense alone) or subordinate (does not)?

“I know”
items.explain: “I know” makes complete sense by itself — a principal clause.

items.prompt:
Is this clause principal (makes sense alone) or subordinate (does not)?

“where gold is found”
items.explain: “where gold is found” cannot stand alone — a subordinate clause.

items.prompt:
Is this clause principal (makes sense alone) or subordinate (does not)?

“she was tired”
items.explain: “she was tired” makes complete sense alone — a principal clause.

items.prompt:
Is this clause principal (makes sense alone) or subordinate (does not)?

“because it rained”
items.explain: “because it rained” cannot stand alone — a subordinate clause.

items.prompt:
Is this clause principal (makes sense alone) or subordinate (does not)?

“the boy studies”
items.explain: “the boy studies” makes complete sense alone — a principal clause.

items.prompt:
Is this clause principal (makes sense alone) or subordinate (does not)?

“when spring comes”
items.explain: “when spring comes” cannot stand alone — a subordinate clause.

items.prompt:
Simple, compound, or complex?

“Dogs bark.”
items.explain: One statement — a simple sentence.

items.prompt:
Simple, compound, or complex?

“Dogs bark, and cats meow.”
items.explain: Two complete statements joined as equals — a compound sentence.

items.prompt:
Simple, compound, or complex?

“I know that you are here.”
items.explain: A subordinate clause (“that you are here”) is built in — a complex sentence.

items.prompt:
Simple, compound, or complex?

“She smiled when he arrived.”
items.explain: A subordinate clause (“when he arrived”) is built in — a complex sentence.

items.prompt:
Simple, compound, or complex?

“Snow fell all night.”
items.explain: One statement — a simple sentence.

items.prompt:
Simple, compound, or complex?

“He tried, but he failed.”
items.explain: Two complete statements joined as equals — a compound sentence.

items.prompt:
Simple, compound, or complex?

“The book that I read was long.”
items.explain: A subordinate clause (“that I read”) is built in — a complex sentence.

items.prompt:
Simple, compound, or complex?

“Birds fly south in winter.”
items.explain: One statement — a simple sentence.

items.prompt:
Which word is the interjection (the exclaiming word)?

“Hurrah! We won the game.”
items.explain: “Hurrah” is thrown in to show feeling — the interjection.

items.prompt:
Which word is the interjection (the exclaiming word)?

“Oh, what a surprise!”
items.explain: “Oh” is thrown in to show feeling — the interjection.

items.prompt:
Which word is the interjection (the exclaiming word)?

“Alas! The ship was lost.”
items.explain: “Alas” is thrown in to show feeling — the interjection.

items.prompt:
Which word is the interjection (the exclaiming word)?

“Ouch! That hurts.”
items.explain: “Ouch” is thrown in to show feeling — the interjection.

items.prompt:
Which word is the interjection (the exclaiming word)?

“Hush! The baby is asleep.”
items.explain: “Hush” is thrown in to show feeling — the interjection.

items.prompt:
Which word is the interjection (the exclaiming word)?

“Wow, look at that!”
items.explain: “Wow” is thrown in to show feeling — the interjection.

items.prompt: Which part of speech names a person, place, or thing?
items.explain: A noun names — a person, place, or thing.

items.prompt: Which part of speech stands in place of a noun?
items.explain: A pronoun stands in for a noun.

items.prompt: Which part of speech asserts action, being, or state?
items.explain: A verb asserts action, being, or state.

items.prompt: Which part of speech describes or defines a noun?
items.explain: An adjective describes or defines a noun.

items.prompt: Which part of speech modifies a verb, adjective, or adverb?
items.explain: An adverb modifies a verb, adjective, or adverb.

items.prompt: Which part of speech shows relation and takes an object?
items.explain: A preposition shows relation and takes an object.

items.prompt: Which part of speech only joins words or groups?
items.explain: A conjunction only joins words or groups.

items.prompt: Which part of speech exclaims sudden feeling?
items.explain: An interjection exclaims sudden feeling.
